label: 论文设计、系统权衡与研究判断

questions.learningObjective: Explain the design intent of Ansor's task scheduler for allocating autotuning budget across subgraphs.
questions.stem: The Ansor paper introduces a 'task scheduler' that allocates autotuning budget across the subgraphs of a full model. Which TWO of the following statements correctly describe the task scheduler's design intent, as argued in the paper?

options.text: The task scheduler distributes budget non-uniformly, favouring subgraphs whose expected marginal improvement × contribution to end-to-end latency is largest, because end-to-end wall-clock time is the objective rather than per-task speedup in isolation.
The task scheduler's motivation is that a uniform-budget baseline (equal time per subgraph) wastes effort on already-optimal or low-contribution subgraphs; the scheduler exists to fix this.
The task scheduler is a runtime scheduler that decides which kernel to launch at inference time; it has nothing to do with autotuning search budget.
The task scheduler enforces that every task must receive at least 10% of the tuning budget so that no task is ever under-tuned.

assumptions: 'Task' means a subgraph carved out for scheduling in Ansor.

questions.subtopic: FlashAttention: IO-awareness, exactness, scope of speedup
questions.learningObjective: Explain FlashAttention's core IO-aware optimization, the mechanism (tiling + online softmax + recomputation), and identify when the speedup is largest.

hardwareContext.architecture: GPU with on-chip SRAM (e.g. A100, H100)
requiredFeatures: large enough SRAM per SM to hold attention block tiles

questions.stem: Which THREE of the following statements about FlashAttention (v1) are correct, per the paper?

options.text: The speedup versus a naive attention kernel is largest in the memory-bound regime (long sequences where HBM traffic dominates) and can be smaller for very short sequences where the naive kernel is compute-bound on the SM.
FlashAttention's backward pass reuses the N×N attention matrix stored during the forward pass; storing this matrix is what makes the backward efficient.

FlashAttention computes attention block-by-block in on-chip SRAM using an online (numerically stable) softmax and never materializes the full N×N attention matrix in HBM; total HBM traffic drops from Θ(N²) to Θ(N²·d/M), where M is the SRAM budget.
FlashAttention produces exact attention outputs (up to floating-point ordering); it does not approximate the softmax or drop entries.

assumptions: SRAM refers to on-chip shared memory / L1 that holds a tile of Q/K/V and running statistics.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish peak (best-case) speedup from geometric-mean speedup and understand the scope-limits of reported paper numbers such as those in GSPMD.
questions.stem: A colleague summarizes GSPMD as 'partitioning gives 2× speedup end-to-end', citing a peak result from one model in the paper. Which TWO statements about interpreting such paper speedups are correct?

options.text: Any speedup reported in a systems paper is a property of the technique alone and is independent of the baseline; comparing against an older framework version is equivalent to comparing against its current version.

A paper's 'peak' speedup is the best-case observation on one (workload, hardware) pair; the geometric-mean speedup across the paper's full workload suite is typically smaller, so summarizing the paper by the peak overstates typical benefits.

Reported speedups are conditioned on that paper's hardware, software stack, workload set and baseline; treating them as a general property of the technique that transfers to arbitrary settings requires additional justification.
Peak and geometric-mean speedup are the same metric computed differently and can be used interchangeably as long as the workload set is identical.

assumptions: The reader understands geometric mean as (∏ speedup_i)^(1/N).
The comparison is across a multi-workload benchmark suite.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Halide paper separates the algorithm (what to compute) from the schedule (how to compute) and identify the design intent behind this separation.
questions.stem: The Halide paper is best known for separating the algorithm (what to compute) from the schedule (how to compute). Which statement best captures the design intent argued in the paper?

options.text: The separation exists so that the compiler can hide the algorithm behind an opaque API; users interact only with schedules.
The separation is required for correctness: only by moving loop order out of the algorithm can Halide guarantee that per-pixel updates remain race-free on multi-core CPUs.

The separation lets a single, portable algorithm be re-scheduled (tiled, vectorized, parallelized, fused, recomputed) without changing its semantics, so many performance-relevant strategies can be explored on each target without rewriting the pipeline.
The separation is a legacy artifact from Halide's origins as a C++ template library; in modern implementations the two parts are merged and the design contribution is largely obsolete.

assumptions: Understanding that a 'schedule' in Halide covers loop order, tiling, storage, parallel/vector directives, and produce-consume relations.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the design intent behind MLIR's multi-level lowering and dialect ecosystem.
questions.stem: The MLIR paper motivates a design with many co-existing dialects at different abstraction levels rather than a single universal IR. Which statement best captures the design intent argued in the paper?

options.text: MLIR argues that a single universal IR is optimal; the multiple dialects are transient artifacts that are collapsed into one representation before any optimization runs.
MLIR's design goal is to be a runtime system that dispatches operations across hardware at execution time; the dialects correspond to different runtimes.

MLIR is designed so each optimization can be expressed at the abstraction level where it is most natural (e.g. tensor-level fusion at a high dialect, tiling at Linalg, code emission at LLVM), with progressive lowering between dialects; the payoff is shared compiler infrastructure reused across domains.
MLIR replaces LLVM as the compilation backend; projects using MLIR no longer emit LLVM IR at any point.

assumptions: Familiarity with MLIR paper §1–§3 and the general pipeline pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish end-to-end model speedup from kernel-level speedup when interpreting the PyTorch 2 paper's `torch.compile` results.

softwareContext.frameworkVersionScope: PyTorch 2.x as reported in the paper

questions.stem: The PyTorch 2 paper reports end-to-end speedups under `torch.compile` on TorchBench-style benchmarks. A reader sees an Inductor-generated Triton kernel that is 3× faster than the eager kernel and infers 'the whole model runs 3× faster'. Which statement most accurately characterizes the reasoning error?

options.text: The reader's error is that Triton kernels never provide speedup over eager on GPUs; the observed 3× must be a measurement artifact and should be discarded.
The reader correctly identifies end-to-end speedup; kernel-level speedup and model-level speedup are always identical when the same benchmark suite is used.

The reader conflates kernel-level and end-to-end speedup. Amdahl's law limits the end-to-end benefit to the fraction of runtime spent in the accelerated kernel; host-side overhead, graph breaks, and non-compiled subgraphs cap the observable end-to-end speedup below the per-kernel factor.
The reader confuses forward and backward pass; end-to-end speedup is defined only for backward-pass time, not the whole model.

assumptions: Familiarity with the PyTorch 2 paper's evaluation methodology.

questions.subtopic: Scope limits of single-paper quantization claims
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the scope limits and common overclaims around single-paper quantization results (SmoothQuant, GPTQ, AWQ).
questions.stem: A colleague summarizes recent quantization work by combining results from SmoothQuant, GPTQ and AWQ into universal claims. Which THREE of the following statements about interpreting these papers are correct?

options.text: An ablation study (e.g. SmoothQuant's migration-factor α) supports the specific mechanism it isolates but does not by itself establish head-to-head superiority over other quantization methods at every setting.

Because all three papers report memory footprint reductions when quantizing to 4-bit, one can conclude that 4-bit quantization always yields ≥3× end-to-end latency speedup regardless of hardware and kernel implementation.

The papers' accuracy results are conditioned on specific model families, sizes, tasks and calibration sets; extending them to 'LLMs in general' (including smaller models, code/math tasks and long-tail benchmarks) requires additional evaluation.

Reported wall-clock speedups depend on the availability of an efficient dequantized-GEMM kernel for the given precision/granularity on the target hardware; the same scheme can be faster on one GPU generation and no faster (or slower) on another.

assumptions: Familiarity with SmoothQuant, GPTQ, AWQ evaluation sections.
Distinction between memory footprint and wall-clock latency.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Triton paper introduces a tile-level IR, positioned between CUDA-thread and pure tensor abstractions.
questions.stem: The Triton paper positions its programming abstraction at the 'tile' (block-of-elements) level rather than at the CUDA thread level. What is the primary design intent argued in the paper?

options.text: Triton targets CPUs and TPUs but not GPUs; the tile IR was designed to hide vendor-specific GPU details that the paper explicitly declines to support.
Triton is a strict superset of CUDA where every CUDA program is also a valid Triton program; the tile abstraction only adds convenience macros without changing what the programmer must reason about.
Triton is a runtime library that dispatches PyTorch operators to hand-written CUDA kernels; the 'tile' terminology refers to caching policies inside the dispatcher.

Programmers write kernels over blocks of elements; the compiler translates tile-level ops into per-thread PTX with coalescing, shared-memory staging and register tiling handled automatically, so users focus on block shapes and memory access patterns rather than per-thread indexing.

questions.subtopic: TVM: real measurement vs analytical cost model
questions.learningObjective: Explain why TVM (and its Ansor/AutoTVM descendants) rely on real hardware measurement rather than a pure analytical cost model to select schedules.
questions.stem: TVM's schedule search relies on on-device measurement (feeding a learned cost model) rather than a pure analytical performance model. Which statement best captures the design rationale argued in the TVM paper?

options.text: Analytical models cannot express any form of loop tiling, so measurement is the only way to compare tiled schedules; without measurement TVM would be forced to emit only untiled code.

On modern accelerators, effective performance depends on hard-to-model factors (cache/coalescing, register pressure, instruction mix, compiler back-end choices) that closed-form models fail to rank reliably at fine granularity, so a measurement-driven (and learned) cost model is used to guide the search.
Measurement is used purely for reproducibility: since analytical models depend on constants that vary by driver version, TVM re-measures every kernel on every deployment to remove that dependency.
The paper argues that a sufficiently detailed analytical model is always superior; measurement is included only as a compatibility path for hardware without a published architecture manual.

assumptions: Familiarity with the TVM paper's autotuning pipeline.

questions.learningObjective: Explain vLLM's PagedAttention design intent: the KV-cache memory-fragmentation problem it targets.
questions.stem: The vLLM paper introduces PagedAttention. What problem, as stated in the paper, is PagedAttention primarily designed to solve?

options.text: It targets KV-cache memory inefficiency: reserving one contiguous buffer per sequence sized to a worst-case length causes internal fragmentation (unused reserved slots) and external fragmentation (holes between sequences); paging KV in fixed-size blocks with a page table lets the serving system fit more concurrent sequences on the same GPU.
It reduces attention FLOPs by paging out cold key/value entries and reloading them only when needed, cutting per-token compute for long sequences.
It eliminates the KV cache entirely by recomputing K and V on demand each decode step, trading extra compute for HBM savings.
It replaces attention with a paged Mixture-of-Experts routing scheme in which each expert operates on one memory page at a time.

assumptions: Reader understands 'internal fragmentation' (unused slots inside a reservation) vs 'external fragmentation' (gaps between reservations).
